newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Iran and S.Africa blame U.S. and Iraq for crisis.
newsitem.headline: Iran and S.Africa blame U.S. and Iraq for crisis.

text.p: Iran's President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and South African President Nelson Mandela on Friday condemned the United States and Iraq, accusing both countries of stoking up the Gulf crisis.
Rafsanjani said the U.S. had boosted tension in Iraq in order to keep a grip on the region, but also blamed Baghdad for giving the Americans the chance.

"There are objectives pursued by the United States by creating such tension and that is to preserve their illegitimate presence in the Persian Gulf and Middle East," he told reporters after talks with Mandela.
"And of course Iraq has provided them with this pretext which is not right, by its invasion of Kuwait and its recent invasion of the Kurds (Kurdish lands)," he said through an interpreter.
Mandela said only the United Nations had the authority to sort out international problems.
"No country is entitled to assume the role of policeman," he said after his 20-minute meeting with the Iranian leader who is on his last leg of a six-nation African tour.
"I do not condone the action of Iraq because...if there is any problem they have with any country, I would expect them to respect the United Nations charter," Mandela said.
Rafsanjani did not comment on a U.N. report on Friday that 30,000 Kurds from northern Iraq had fled to Iran.
U.S. ships and assault planes closed in on Iraq on Friday preparing to punish President Saddam Hussein.
Mandela, who brushed aside U.S. displeasure over his decision to host Rafsanjani for a full state visit, said no country had the right to dictate South Africa's foreign policy.
"We are not prepared to do that at the expense of our friends who were with us when we were all alone, when many superpowers were supporting our enemies, the apartheid regime.
"Those who were with us when we were all alone will continue to be our friends."

The two presidents said officials from both governments had been negotiating several agreements over trade, industry, science and technology during Rafsanjani's two-day visit, and hoped some deals would be signed before he left later on Friday.
The deals could help rectify a trade imbalance favouring Iran. South Africa has depended on Iran for two-thirds of its crude oil for which it pays about five billion rand ($1.12 billion) annually.
Iran last year bought South African goods worth only 145.7 million rand ($32.5 million).

Rafsanjani said Iran would be ready to accept a deal to store at least 15 million barrels of Iranian crude at the Central Energy Fund's (CEF) 45-million barrel depot at Saldanha Bay north of Cape Town, if South Africa was willing.
Asked about rumours that Iran was among the Moslem countries funding Islamic fundamentalist groups in South Africa, Mandela said he was not aware of the allegations.
"(But) if they do so, there is no reason why we should complain. We are a democracy and any particular group or party that tries to raise funds wherever they feel, they can raise those funds."
